what_its_for: Fluorouracil is a cancer-fighting medicine (chemotherapy). The injectable form (given through a vein) is used to treat cancers of the colon, rectum, breast, stomach, and pancreas. The cream or solution you put on your skin is used to treat certain skin conditions like actinic keratoses (rough, scaly patches caused by sun damage) and some types of skin cancer (basal cell carcinoma). It works by slowing or stopping the growth of abnormal cells.
how_to_take: INJECTABLE FORM: This is given by a nurse or doctor through a needle in your vein (IV) in a clinic or hospital. You will NOT give this to yourself at home unless specifically trained and instructed to do so with a special infusion pump. CREAM OR SOLUTION (for skin): Wash your hands before and after applying. Use a clean fingertip, cotton-tipped applicator, or glove to apply a thin layer only to the affected skin area your doctor pointed out. Do NOT apply it to your eyes, mouth, lips, or inside your nose. Avoid getting it on healthy surrounding skin as much as possible. Do NOT cover the treated area with a bandage or tight dressing unless your doctor tells you to.
dosing: INJECTABLE: Your doctor will calculate your exact dose based on your body size, type of cancer, and overall health. It is usually given in cycles — for example, daily for several days, then a rest period. Follow your oncology team's schedule exactly. CREAM OR SOLUTION: Most people apply it once or twice a day for several weeks. Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to use and for how long. Do not use more than directed — using too much can cause serious skin irritation. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's specific instructions because doses vary widely from person to person.
missed_dose: INJECTABLE: If you miss a scheduled infusion appointment, call your oncology clinic right away to reschedule. Do not try to 'make up' a missed dose on your own. CREAM OR SOLUTION: If you forget to apply a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed application and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT apply a double dose to make up for the one you missed.
storage: INJECTABLE (if stored at home with a pump): Keep it at room temperature (around 59–77°F / 15–25°C) unless your pharmacist gives you different instructions. Keep it away from light. CREAM OR SOLUTION: Store at room temperature. Keep the cap tightly closed. Keep ALL forms of fluorouracil away from children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about proper disposal options.
what_to_avoid: Sun exposure: Avoid direct sunlight and UV lamps (tanning beds) during treatment and for several weeks after, especially on treated skin areas. Fluorouracil makes your skin very sensitive to the sun. Always use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) and wear protective clothing. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT use fluorouracil if you are pregnant — it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for some time after. Do not breastfeed while using this medicine. Touching others: Wash treated skin areas before close contact with others, especially children or pregnant women, to avoid accidental transfer of the cream. Live vaccines: Avoid live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine) during chemotherapy treatment without first asking your doctor. Other medicines and supplements: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take. Some medicines (like metronidazole, cimetidine, and leucovorin) can interact with fluorouracil.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (a sign of serious infection), chills or shaking, severe diarrhea (more than 4 loose stools a day) or stomach pain, vomiting that will not stop or prevents you from drinking fluids, mouth sores that make it very hard to eat or drink, chest pain, shortness of breath, or rapid heartbeat, signs of a blood clot such as sudden leg pain, swelling, or redness, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, unusual bruising or bleeding, yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), severe skin reaction — blistering, peeling, oozing, or extreme pain in treated skin areas, or signs of a serious allergic reaction — rash all over your body, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you notice your skin reactions seem unusually severe, if treated skin is not healing, or if you have any concerns.
when_it_works: CREAM OR SOLUTION on skin: You will likely notice skin changes — redness, peeling, and irritation — within the first 1–2 weeks. This is normal and usually means the medicine is working. Full healing of the skin typically takes 1–2 months after you finish the full course of treatment. The skin may look worse before it looks better. INJECTABLE (chemotherapy): It may take several weeks or months of treatment cycles before your doctor can tell how well the medicine is working. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular check-ups, lab tests, and scans. Be patient and keep all your appointments.
special_populations: Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially mouth sores, diarrhea, and low blood cell counts. Close monitoring is important. Children: Safety in children has not been well established; use is determined case by case by a specialist. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments may be needed. Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions. Pregnancy: This medicine MUST NOT be used during pregnancy. It can cause serious birth defects or fetal death. Women of childbearing age must use reliable contraception during treatment and for at least 3–6 months after stopping (your doctor will advise the exact timeframe). Men should also use contraception and avoid fathering a child during and for several months after treatment. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while using fluorouracil. DPD enzyme deficiency: Some people have a rare genetic condition called DPD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase) deficiency that prevents their body from breaking down fluorouracil safely, which can lead to life-threatening side effects. Ask your doctor if you should be tested before starting treatment.
